title: Rabdentse, the ruined second capital of Sikkim
meta_description: Rabdentse near Pelling was Sikkim's capital from 1670: a royal murder, a Gorkha raid in 1788, the judges' stones and chortens, and how to walk there.
summary: Rabdentse, about 3 km from Pelling, was the second capital of Sikkim from 1670, taken by a Gorkha army in 1788 and abandoned for Tumlong after 1793. Today it is a quiet ASI-protected ruin of walls, chortens and judges' stones, reached by a 15-minute forest walk for a small fee.

sections.heading: Why the court moved to this ridge
paras: Sikkim's first capital was Yuksom, where Phuntsog Namgyal was crowned in 1642. We tell that story in our Yuksom guide. When he died in 1670, his son Tensung Namgyal, the second Chogyal, moved the court to a ridge, about 35 km away by today's road, above the Rangeet valley. That ridge is Rabdentse, a short walk from today's Pelling.

Wikipedia dates Rabdentse's time as capital to 1670–1814. The records we can check do not give Tensung's reason for the move. Stand on the ruins on a clear morning, though, and the site explains itself. The ridge drops away on three sides, the Rangeet valley spreads out below, and the Kangchenjunga range fills the skyline to the north. It is a place that is easy to watch from and hard to approach.

For more than a century the kings of Sikkim held court here. The palace stood on the highest ground, with chortens for worship, a seat of justice and a ceremonial entrance. Below it lay the farms and villages that fed the court.

sections.heading: Chakdor Namgyal and his half-sister
paras: The best-known story from Rabdentse belongs to the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, born in 1686. He came to the throne in 1700 as a boy. His elder half-sister, Pende Ongmu, a daughter of Tensung by another wife, opposed his succession. According to Wikipedia's accounts, she called in help from Bhutan and drove him out.

The young king fled to Lhasa. There, Wikipedia records, he lived under the protection of the sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, who granted him estates at Shigatse and Yamdrok. He spent his exile in Buddhist study and married in Tibet. Bhutanese forces held parts of Sikkim until 1708, and Sikkim lost land east of the Teesta in this period. Chakdor came home and took back his throne.

His reign is remembered for building as much as for intrigue. Pemayangtse Monastery, which looks down on Rabdentse from the next hill, was enlarged under him in 1705, and Tashiding Monastery was extended in 1717 in his name. Pende Ongmu did not give up. Wikipedia says she contacted the Deb Raja of Bhutan to send a force to kill Chakdor, but the minister Yugthing Tishey uncovered the plot in time.

sections.heading: The death at Ralang in 1716
paras: In 1716 Pende Ongmu tried again, and this time she succeeded. Wikipedia's account says she hired a Tibetan doctor to attend the king at Ralang, away from the capital. The doctor persuaded Chakdor that he needed bloodletting, then opened a main artery and let him bleed to death. Popular tellings in Sikkim place the killing at the hot spring near Ralang, where the king had gone to rest. The written accounts we checked say only that it happened at Ralang, on a royal holiday.

Lama Jigme Pawo found the dying king and later reported his death. Both the doctor and Pende Ongmu were executed. Wikipedia's Namchi article says she was caught and strangled at Namchi. Chakdor was about 30 years old. His son Gyurmed Namgyal, born during the Tibetan exile, became the fourth Chogyal.

sections.heading: The Gorkha wars and the move to Tumlong
paras: Rabdentse's end came from the west. In the late 18th century the Gorkha kingdom of Nepal was expanding fast. In 1788, Wikipedia records, a Nepali Gorkha army invaded Sikkim, took the Limbu lands of Limbuana and stormed Rabdentse. The Chogyal, Tenzing Namgyal, fled to Tibet, the second time a Sikkimese king had gone into exile from this ridge.

His son Tshudpud Namgyal returned in 1793. He judged Rabdentse too close to the Nepal border and moved the capital east to Tumlong, in what is now North Sikkim. Later Tumlong gave its name to the 1861 Treaty of Tumlong with the British. Rabdentse was left to the forest, and over two centuries the trees, rain and earthquakes did the rest.

The map changed again within a generation. In the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16 Sikkim sided with the British East India Company, and the Treaty of Titalia in 1817 gave back to Sikkim much of the land Nepal had taken. By then the court was settled at Tumlong, and Rabdentse never became a capital again. That is why the ruins feel so complete in their emptiness: nothing was built over them.

sections.heading: What the ruins look like today
paras: Do not expect a palace. What survives are stone wall stubs, raised platforms and three chortens, cleared and kept tidy by the Archaeological Survey of India, which protects the site as a monument of national importance. Walk in with the plan in your head and the stones start to make sense.

The first structure you meet is the Taphap Chorten, the old entrance. Visitors to the palace dismounted here and took off their hats before going on, and many people still pause at it today. Further in is Namphogang, a stone seat made of three standing stones where judges sat to hear cases. Beyond that rise the walls of the palace itself. Wikipedia describes a northern wing where the royal family lived and a southern wing used for public audiences. Three chortens stand on a raised terrace; here the royal family offered incense to the deities.
The view is the real reward. On a clear day from October to December the whole Kangchenjunga range lines up above the ruins, and Pemayangtse's roofs sit on the hill just above you.

sections.heading: Walking there from Pelling
paras: Rabdentse is about 3 km from Upper Pelling, on the road down towards Gyalshing. A decorated gate on the Pelling–Gyalshing road marks the start, close to the turning for Pemayangtse. From the gate a paved and stepped path runs through forest to the ruins. It takes about 15 minutes each way at an easy pace, with a few gentle ups and downs.

From Upper Pelling you can walk the whole way in about 45 minutes, mostly downhill on the road; the return is uphill. A shared jeep between Pelling and Gyalshing costs ₹50–80 a seat, indicative 2026, and can drop you at the gate. If you hire a car, Rabdentse fits into a half-day Pelling round with Pemayangtse and Sanga Choeling for ₹1,500–2,500 per car, indicative 2026. Plan 1–1.5 hours at the ruins themselves.

The order matters. We suggest Pemayangtse first at about 8 am, then the short walk down the road to the Rabdentse gate while the light is still clear. By 11 am cloud often rises from the Rangeet valley and the mountains go. Families with small children manage the path easily, and the open terraces at the ruins are a safe place for them to run about, though the edges of the ridge are unfenced in places. Photographers should bring a wide lens for the chortens with the range behind.
list: Entry: ₹25–50 for Indian visitors and more for foreign nationals, indicative 2026; ASI fees change, so check current status before you travel.
Hours: roughly daytime only, about 8 am to 5 pm; arrive early for the clearest mountain views.
Combine with Pemayangtse, which sits on the hill directly above, and you need no extra transport.
Wear shoes with grip; the forest path is slippery after rain and in the monsoon months.
Do not climb on the walls or chortens, and walk around the chortens clockwise.
There is no café at the site; carry water and keep all litter with you.

faqs.a: Rabdentse is famous as the second capital of the Kingdom of Sikkim, from 1670 until the court moved to Tumlong after 1793; Wikipedia dates its time as capital to 1670–1814. Today it is a ruin of palace walls, three chortens, the Taphap Chorten entrance and the Namphogang judges' stones, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, with wide views of the Kangchenjunga range.

faqs.q: How far is Rabdentse from Pelling
faqs.a: About 3 km from Upper Pelling on the road towards Gyalshing. From the gate on the Pelling–Gyalshing road it is a 15-minute walk through forest to the ruins. You can walk all the way from Pelling in about 45 minutes, take a shared jeep for ₹50–80 to the gate, or include it in a half-day car tour, indicative 2026.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Rabdentse ruins
faqs.a: Expect ₹25–50 for Indian visitors and a higher fee for foreign nationals, indicative 2026. Rabdentse is an ASI monument, and ASI fees and payment methods change from time to time, so carry cash as well as a phone for digital payment, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why was the capital moved from Rabdentse
faqs.a: Because it was too exposed to Nepal. In 1788 a Gorkha army from Nepal invaded Sikkim and took Rabdentse, and the Chogyal fled to Tibet. When his son Tshudpud Namgyal returned in 1793 he judged the ridge too close to the Nepal border and moved the capital east to Tumlong, in what is now North Sikkim.

According to Wikipedia's accounts, his half-sister Pende Ongmu hired a Tibetan doctor who attended the king at Ralang in 1716, persuaded him to be bled and let him bleed to death. Popular tellings place this at the hot spring near Ralang. The doctor and Pende Ongmu were both executed; one account says she was strangled at Namchi.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at Rabdentse
faqs.a: Plan 1 to 1.5 hours, including the 15-minute walk in and out from the road gate. That leaves time to read the ASI boards, sit by the chortens and wait for cloud to lift off Kangchenjunga. Most people pair it with Pemayangtse Monastery on the hill above in a single morning.

faqs.q: Is the walk to Rabdentse difficult
faqs.a: No. It is an easy 15-minute walk on a paved and stepped forest path with a few gentle slopes, fine for children and most seniors. The stones can be slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip. Walking from Upper Pelling adds about 45 minutes downhill on the road and a steady climb back.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Rabdentse
faqs.a: Early morning from October to December gives the clearest views of the Kangchenjunga range above the ruins. March to May is fine but haze often builds by late morning. In the monsoon, June to September, the path is wet and leech-prone and the mountains usually hide. The site is open in daylight only.

faqs.q: Can I combine Rabdentse with other sites
faqs.a: Yes. Pemayangtse Monastery is on the hill just above the gate, and Sanga Choeling, the Chenrezig statue and the Pelling Skywalk are a short drive away. A half-day car for all of them costs ₹1,500–2,500, indicative 2026. Yuksom, the first capital, makes a good next stop, about 35 km away.
